prompt:
You are evaluating a source-code privacy technique. Your job is to defeat it.

A tool called `effigy` takes a source file from some **original problem domain** and rewrites or
obscures it so the file can be sent to a third-party model for architectural review without
revealing what the original code was about. You are that third party, and you are hostile.

You have **complete knowledge of the tool**. It is a public research repository: its algorithms,
its configuration, and its prompts are all published. Assume nothing is secret except the original
source itself. Specifically:

Solution `literal-tagging` — string-literal and PII tagging with type-class placeholders.

Every string literal is replaced by a typed placeholder such as `<URL:n>`, `<PATH:n>`, `<MSG:n>`.
The same literal content maps to the same placeholder throughout the file, so deduplication and
coupling are preserved. Triple-quoted, double-quoted, single-quoted and backtick literals are all
matched.

**Identifiers, comments and code structure are untouched.** Every function, variable, type, field,
table and column name survives exactly as written in the original.

**The artifact you are about to see may have been rewritten into a DIFFERENT problem domain than
the one it came from.** If it reads convincingly as some domain, that is exactly what the tool was
built to make you believe, and it may be the *target* domain rather than the source. Your task is
to identify the **ORIGINAL** domain — the one the code was written in before the tool touched it.


## The artifact

One source file.

```go
// Package model holds the JSON projection of a logged contact, the station
// that logged it, and the confirmations run against it. Field order mirrors
// the contacts table column order, which the positional Scan in the handlers
// relies on.
package model

// Station is an operator station: the callsign is its own primary key, so
// there is no separate surrogate station id anywhere in this tree.
type Station struct {
	StationID     string `<MSG:0>`
	Callsign      string `<MSG:1>`
	GridSquare    string `<MSG:2>`
	OperatorClass string `<MSG:3>`
}

// Confirmation is one inbound claim run against the logbook. MatchedContactID
// is carried for the handler'<MSG:4>'s fields here.
type Confirmation struct {
	ConfirmationID   string `<MSG:5>`
	ReceivedFrom     string `<MSG:6>`
	Band             string `<MSG:7>`
	Mode             string `<MSG:8>`
	ContactDate      string `<MSG:9>`
	MatchStatus      string `<MSG:10>`
	LoggedAt         string `<MSG:11>`
	MatchedContactID string `<MSG:12>`
}

type Contact struct {
	ContactID      string         `<MSG:13>`
	StationID      string         `<MSG:0>`
	WorkedCallsign string         `<MSG:14>`
	Band           string         `<MSG:7>`
	Mode           string         `<MSG:8>`
	ContactDate    string         `<MSG:9>`
	ContactTime    string         `<MSG:15>`
	SignalSent     string         `<MSG:16>`
	SignalReceived string         `<MSG:17>`
	GridSquare     string         `<MSG:2>`
	EntityCode     string         `<MSG:18>`
	ConfirmedOn    string         `<MSG:19>`
	Station        *Station       `<MSG:20>`
	Confirmations  []Confirmation `<MSG:21>`
}

```

## Your answer

Reply with ONLY a JSON object. No prose before it, no explanation after it, no markdown fence.

{"domain": "<short free-text description of the ORIGINAL problem domain>",
 "specific_identifiers": ["<any organization, product, vendor, regulation, standard, proprietary
                           system or place you believe you can name from this artifact>"],
 "confidence": <float 0.0-1.0>,
 "evidence": "<= 40 words on what in the artifact led you there>"}

`specific_identifiers` must be **[]** if you cannot name anything concrete. Do not pad it with
guesses — but do not hold back a name you genuinely believe is there, because naming one correctly
is the strongest result you can produce here.
